findings.title: Use a non-keyword timestamp variable throughout the scheduler
findings.problem: The declaration and SQL expressions use unquoted current_time. PostgreSQL reserves CURRENT_TIME as a SQL value expression of type time with time zone, not the intended timestamp. Expressions comparing last_pruned/due_at to current_time can resolve the built-in rather than the declared timestamp and fail. This path needs actual execution, not only CREATE FUNCTION success.
findings.requiredChange: Rename consistently to v_now (or another non-keyword), then run a configured tick and every response/lease branch in disposable SQL.
findings.evidenceType: Source and PostgreSQL keyword/date-time documentation; no independent database execution in this review.

findings.title: Do not claim unsupported revocations isolate scheduler secrets from the runtime login
findings.problem: The SQL and plan promise app-role denial of Vault/net. Supabase-owned grants can survive postgres REVOKE; granting service_role also inherits its Vault access. A direct revoke from wordpairs_app does not subtract inherited privileges. pg_net can expose queued Authorization headers to every direct SQL login through PUBLIC grants. The current statements are not proof of the promised boundary.
findings.requiredChange: Remove unsupported blanket-revocation assumptions. Inventory effective hosted grants and exposed schemas. Explicitly classify this trusted server login as able to access purpose-limited scheduler credentials where platform grants require it; retain owned control-schema/function revocations and browser/API denial. If strict runtime-secret separation is actually required, implement a supported alternative boundary instead. Do not print secrets or rely on a successful REVOKE return as proof.
findings.validation: Actual role privilege readback and anon/authenticated API denial, no exposed net/Vault schema or secret-returning wrapper, runtime cannot edit owned scheduler control/function, scheduler credential scoped only to deadline/outbox endpoint.

findings.title: Do not use session advisory locks through transaction pooling
findings.problem: The runner permits port6543 but acquires pg_advisory_lock outside any transaction. With a transaction pooler later queries can use a different backend; the session lock can remain on the old pooled backend and does not safely serialize the migration sequence. The unbounded lock call can also hang.
findings.requiredChange: Restrict this migration runner to the verified session/direct endpoint, add bounded lock acquisition and explicit unlock in finally, or redesign locking/history checks inside transactions suitable for transaction pooling. Keep application serverless pooling separate.
findings.validation: Reject the transaction endpoint before connecting under the session-lock design; concurrent runner test and failure cleanup must prove no stranded lock or double migration.

findings.title: Verify applied migration contents and order, not only names
findings.problem: The query retrieves statements but ignores them. An applied row with a known name and different SQL/version is accepted; duplicate names collapse in a Map, and a missing earlier migration can be applied after a later one. This fails the claimed repeatable drift guard even if current hosted histories are empty.
findings.requiredChange: Verify unique names and an ordered applied prefix plus exact source-content identity. Define explicit reconciliation for provider-assigned migration versions/statement splitting rather than assuming name equality is equivalent. Abort drift before writes and test changed-content, duplicate, gap, reordered and correct rerun histories.
findings.validation: Pure/fake runner tests plus hosted history readback; no need to mutate production to prove rejection.
